output.title: HTTP header injection vulnerabilities and prevention techniques
output.description:
In HTTP, "Referer" (a misspelling of "Referrer") is an optional HTTP header field that identifies the address of the web page (i.e., the URI or IRI) from which the resource has been requested. By checking the referrer, the server providing the new web page can see where the request originated.
In the most common situation, this means that when a user clicks a hyperlink in a web browser, causing the browser to send a request to the server holding the destination web page, the request may include the Referer field, which indicates the last page the user was on (the one where they clicked the link).
Web sites and web servers log the content of the received Referer field to identify the web page from which the user followed a link, for promotional or statistical purposes. This entails a loss of privacy for the user and may introduce a security risk. To mitigate security risks, browsers have been steadily reducing the amount of information sent in Referer. As of March 2021, by default Chrome, Chromium-based Edge, Firefox, Safari default to sending only the origin in cross-origin requests, stripping out everything but the domain name.

parameters.query: HTTP header injection vulnerabilities and prevention techniques

output.description:
HTTP header injection vulnerabilities occur when an attacker is able to manipulate the headers of an HTTP request or response in order to inject malicious content. This can lead to various security risks such as cross-site scripting (XSS), HTTP response splitting, and cache poisoning.

To prevent HTTP header injection vulnerabilities, it is important to validate and sanitize user input before using it in headers. In the provided code snippet, the `isValidHeaderValue` function uses a regular expression to check if the header value contains only printable ASCII characters (32-126) and certain allowed characters like commas and semicolons. Additionally, it ensures that the value does not contain carriage return or line feed characters (\r\n), which can be used for header injection attacks.

Other prevention techniques for HTTP header injection vulnerabilities include:
1. Encoding user input: Encode user input before using it in headers to prevent special characters from being interpreted as part of the header.
2. Limiting input length: Limit the length of input allowed in headers to prevent buffer overflow attacks.
3. Using secure coding practices: Follow secure coding practices such as input validation, output encoding, and parameterized queries to prevent injection attacks.
4. Implementing content security policies (CSP): Use CSP headers to restrict the sources of content that can be loaded on a web page, reducing the risk of XSS attacks.

By implementing these prevention techniques and validating user input properly, you can reduce the risk of HTTP header injection vulnerabilities in your application.
